blocks.text: Knock. A clear ring, like a bell with a thumb on it.
Knock. Clear.
Knock. Flat. Dull as a dropped brick.
I've tapped every stand in the Kilnyard Drum twenty times since the Run began. Yesterday the Last Stand rang true as a bell. This morning it rocks in its bed when I lean on it.
Stone doesn't loosen itself overnight. Somebody has been down here.
And the match is in three hours.

I came down at first light to knock the walls, the way I promised myself on the walk home from Wellhead. Walls first. Dry. Kiln-warm at the back where the old flue runs, cool by the stair. No sweat on them anywhere. Pace will hold at five tonight.
Then, because I'm a mason and I can't leave a job half done, the floor.

Eighteen stands ring the way they've always rung. The nineteenth, the Last Stand, under our Last Plate, sits a hair proud on its left corner. I put my heel on it and it tips. A finger's breadth. Enough to throw a draw. Enough to throw a Damper.

I lie flat and put my cheek nearly to the stone. The bed joint on the left side has been raked out, neat, a palm deep, and the dust brushed back in over the gap to hide it. Whoever did this knew where to put a tool so it wouldn't mark the face. Whoever did this knew stone.
I could re-bed it in an hour. Lime, a mallet, a level. My hands are already reaching for my bag.
I sit on them.

Tampering with a stand is forfeit and a season's ban. The rule doesn't say tampering to make it worse. Mend it myself and it's my word that it was ever broken, and my word belongs to a nineteen-year-old with a bailiff's notice on the door.
The Warden comes down at noon with his lanterns and his tell-weight. He's a grey, careful man with a voice like a parish clerk, and he listens to all of it with his head on one side.
"Rocks, you say."
"Stand on it."
He doesn't. He looks at it. Then he looks at me.
"This floor was certified at the start of the Run, Halloway. A certified floor is sound."
"It was sound yesterday. Somebody's raked the bed. Look at the joint."
"Stands settle."
"Not overnight. Not on one corner. Not with the dust swept back in after." I hear myself getting loud, and stop. "Only a Chapter Warden can prove tampering. That's you. I'm asking you to look."
He smiles at me, very kindly. That's worse than if he'd shouted.

"I'm here to referee a match, not to lift a floor three hours before one. The floor is certified. You may play it, or you may forfeit." He nods at my bag. "And I'd keep your chisels buckled up, Halloway. A mason's chisel near a stand is a very poor look."
He goes to hang his lanterns. Four hooks. Four Dampers.
Sef has been behind me the whole time. He walks round to my right without being asked.

"Three things," he says. "One, he's not going to look. Two, if he won't look, it isn't broken. Not on paper. Three, if it isn't broken on paper, we play round it. Four things. Four, I'm registering a reserve."
"We haven't got a reserve."
"We have now." He jerks his chin at the stair.

Jory Tewkes is sitting halfway down it, swinging her boots. Fifteen, the kiln-master's niece, sleeves black with soot because she lives in the yard above us. She's watched every drill night from that step and copied every one of Dov's throws into her own throat when she thought nobody was listening. I was listening. She's not bad.
"Reserve Caller," Sef tells the Warden, who writes it on his sheet. "Jory Tewkes. So Dov can stand as Damper at a Half if we ever need him to."
Dov is just coming down the stair with his bag over his shoulder. He stops dead on the bottom step.
"Stand as what?"
"If we ever need you to," says Sef.

"I'm a Caller. I'm *the* Caller. Half that gallery pays a crown to hear me. Nobody pays a crown to watch a man stand still and breathe in." He laughs, too loud for the room. "Put the child on the Last Stand, if you're so keen on her."
"Nobody's going on the Last Stand," I say. "It rocks."
Dov looks at the Last Stand, and then away from it fast, the way you look away from a dog you don't trust. He doesn't say another word until the bloom's up. For Dov, that's a very long time.
Jory waves at him. He doesn't wave back.
Sef calls the plan in the kiln yard, on his fingers.

Marten comes off the Last Stand. With nobody on it there's no Hand-Still, no stopping a Peal once it starts. We take that. Mrs. Oduya walks the peg hard all night, so their strikes land off. And I re-map.

I do it on my knees with the floor chart and a stub of chalk. Every pair I've used this Run with a foot on the Last Stand comes out. That's three of our best. What's left is wing pairs: good for notes thrown wide, no use at all for notes thrown down the middle.
Mrs. Oduya reads the chart over my shoulder.
"You have made a very fine pie crust, Wren Halloway," she says. "With a hole in the middle."
"I know."
"So will they."
"Pace five," says the Warden.
I could have told him that.

Malthouse's Scribe is a long, quiet woman with a maltster's stoop who never watches the plates, only our feet. Sef calls her the Rake inside a sentence and doesn't stop to explain. Their heavy Caller is a red-faced man with a voice like a barrel rolling downhill. The Mash.
It takes the Rake two throws.

Her first goes wide at our left wing. I read the lead-in up through my soles, call the wing pair, face Marten and give him the count with my whole mouth. "Three. Two. Draw." His draw and mine land together. The note dies in the air between us, a clean nothing.
The Warden's rod goes to my stand, then his. "Nothing, Halloway. Nothing, Sallow."
"Ghost!" shouts somebody in the gallery, and half of them laugh, and half of them don't.
Her second throw goes straight down the middle, over the empty Last Stand, and Peals.
The Rake doesn't smile. She looks at the empty stand, then at me, and nods once, like she's found the soft brick in a wall.
Dov answers with the Lamplighter. One each.
Then the Mash.

He Raises from Malthouse's left-hand stand and his lead-in comes up through the floor heavy and sure, right on our peg, straight down the middle where I've got no pair left. Nothing to null. So I do the only other thing. I step into the beam to block it, because a body takes a weight off whatever passes through it.
The front hits me in the chest like a sack of wet sand off a cart.
Then I'm on the floor.

Not hurt. Off. Shoulder on cold stone, the glow crawling away from me toward our plate. I'm back on my stand before it's gone another pace. Stepping back onto your own stand isn't hush-stepping. But a knocked-off Damper can't draw again until the next throw, so I stand there with my palms open and nothing to do with them.
Weight four going in. Three after me. It finds Mrs. Oduya's peg anyway.
One. Two. Three. Peal.
Two to one, Malthouse.
"Off the middle, all of you!" Sef shouts. Loud. Much louder than he needs. "It's rotten, keep off it!"
The Rake hears. Of course she does. That's why he said it.
Dov Peals the Ferret before the Half, and we go to the Long Ground level at two each, with a hole in our floor that everybody in the Drum can see.
The Long Ground clears nothing from me. I've drawn nothing to clear. I spend it on my knees again, chalk in hand, while Sef talks.

"Three things. One, the Rake goes back to whatever worked. Every Scribe does. Two, every throw she's sent at the hole has come off the Mash's left-hand stand. It's his good side, he likes the angle. Three." He stops. Points at my chalk. "Wren. You've got a face on."
I have. Because from the Mash's left-hand stand, the beam comes in at a slant.

The two stands either side of the Last Stand sit three paces apart, a pace and a half each side of it. Come at them straight and they're the same distance along the beam. Useless. Come at them on the Mash's slant, and the near one sits a pace and a fifth closer along the path than the far one. And both are inside the beam. Only by a hand's width each. But inside.
Half a wave, a pace and a fifth. So a whole wave of two paces and two-fifths.
"Mrs. Oduya. At pace five, what note runs two and two-fifths?"
She doesn't even look up. "Two semitones above where my peg sits now."
"Can you walk it there?"

"In two Breaths, Wren Halloway." Then she does look up, and something like delight crosses her face. "Ah. Any note that means to Peal must come within a semitone of my peg. So they must throw your note, or score nothing. It is like laying the table so the guest can only sit in one chair."
"Four things," says Sef, and puts up a fourth finger. "Four. That."
Marten has been watching my mouth the whole time. "Aye, well," he says. "Either side of the hole, then."
"Either side of the hole. On my count."
"Your count," he says. "Aye."
Second Half. Sef makes us pay for the bait first.
He keeps Marten and me out on the wings, body-blocking wide, and the Rake sends the Mash at the hole again off his good side. It goes in clean. Three to two, Malthouse. The gallery groans.

Dov sets his feet with his face set hard, and Raises, and throws the Widowmaker: high, long, a bend on the end like a hook going into a fish. Last time out it rattled wide and he blamed the plate. This time it lands on their peg dead centre.
"The Widowmaker!" he tells the gallery, both arms up. "You're welcome!"
Three each.

Mrs. Oduya walks our peg one semitone at the Breath. Then another. The pitch peg sits on the rail where everyone can see it, the Rake included. She reads it and shrugs. Of course she does. She's not aiming at the peg. She's aiming at the hole.
Sef gives the call.

Marten and I take the two stands either side of the Last Stand. The empty stone sits between us like a missing tooth. From the Malthouse end it must look exactly like two frightened Dampers who won't stand on rotten stone, guarding the gap from either side and hoping. The worst a straight-up doubling could cost us is Marks.
The Rake looks at us. Looks at the hole.
The Mash steps onto his left-hand stand.

I put my weight through my heels and spread my toes on the stone. The Raise goes up. His lead-in comes up through the floor ahead of the air and settles right where Mrs. Oduya's peg is waiting. Right inside our band.
I turn my face to Marten. Make my mouth big.
"Three. Two. Draw."
We draw in the same instant. Palms out, breath in.
The note doesn't arrive. It just stops, in the stone between us, like a door closing in another house. No ring in my hands. No hum in my teeth. Nothing.
The Warden's rod, my stand, then Marten's. "Nothing, Halloway. Nothing, Sallow."
Underfoot the Kilnyard floor is quiet and very still. I don't wait to find out whether it stays that way. I keep my eyes on Sef.
Dov takes our next throw. The Long Goodnight, slow and fat and right on their peg.
Four to three.

The Malthouse Scribe has one throw left and she knows what she's looking at now. I watch her think about it. A wing, cold, to beat my feet? But a cold throw drifts, and a drift off our peg rattles, and a rattle is nothing. She needs a Peal, so she needs our peg, and our peg is ours.
She sends the Mash at the hole from his good side one last time, because it's the only door she's got.
"Three. Two. Draw."
Nothing. Again.
"Nothing, Halloway. Nothing, Sallow."
Four to three, Kilnyard.
The gallery doesn't shout "Ghost!" this time. It just makes a long low sound, like a kiln door opening.
Afterwards Sef pays out the gate. One crown for me. At home I put it in the tin over the banker and count. Five of thirty-eight.
Next morning I go back down with a lamp to look at that bed joint in daylight, or what passes for daylight under a kiln. Sef is already at the foot of the stair, standing very still.
"Wren," he says. "Look up."
The lintel over the Drum door is blank.
The two figures on their stands, the wave-marks across the gap between them, the row of deep and shallow notches. Gone. Chiselled off in the night, flat and clean.

I put my palm on it. Fresh stone dust in the cracks of the step below. A bolster, drawn level, a good steady hand, a bed as true as anything I've ever laid. Whoever did it didn't hack. They dressed it. Mason's work. The same kind of hands that know how to rake a bed joint without marking the face.
I don't much like lintels. I like this one less with nothing on it.
"The stand," I say. "Then this."
"Then this," says Sef.
He doesn't take out his notebook. He lifts one knuckle and taps the doorframe, slow and sure, deep and shallow. Every notch. In order. Not one pause to think. Not one look at anything but the stone.
When he's done, he puts his hands in his pockets.
Somebody with the run of this Drum wanted that carving gone, badly enough to come back for it the night after the stand.
And the only copy left is in Sef's head. And I'm starting to notice that Sef never looks at his own notebook.
